question: The site that the Roman municipal authorities have earmarked for the capital’s new incinerator had, until 18 November 20221, been off-limits to waste treatment plants because it had been included2 in the Lazio Region’s environmental restrictions system3 as part of the process of drawing the boundaries of the protection area for the Laurentino water wells (which provide drinking water to the town of Ardea4).

In March 2025, the Lazio Region decided to call off the Laurentino protection area mapping procedure5. The decision was taken at the request of ACEA, a multi-utility company which manages the water network and is controlled by the municipal authorities6.

ACEA cited the 20167 discovery of chlorine-based pollutants in the Laurentino aquifer and the possibility of switching to other (as-yet-unspecified) sources of water as being the reasons behind its decision. The Laurentino wells9 will continue to supply Ardea8 on an indefinite basis.

ACEA’s request does nothing to address the damage that has already been done to the Laurentino wells and could, in fact, expose the aquifer to new sources of pollution. It could, additionally, constitute a conflict of interest, as ACEA heads the consortium responsible for building the Rome incinerator10.

Having regard for infringement procedures INFR (2025) 2207 and INFR (2026) 2038 and two cases similar to the one in question – namely the recent measures authorising the construction on the outskirts of Rome of the Salone and Casal Selce11 biodigesters, the latter of which is the subject of an ongoing appeal before the Court of Justice of the European Union12 – could the Commission clarify whether, in relation to the matter at hand, Italy is correctly applying the Water Framework Directive?

answer: The Water Framework Directive (WFD) (1) requires Member States to prevent the deterioration of status of water bodies and to carry out a prior assessment of the potential impacts of a new project if it may pose a risk in this respect. The assessment can be combined with an environmental impact assessment (EIA) or other assessments required under EU or national law.

Article 7 WFD requires Member States to identify and monitor the water bodies used for abstracting drinking water, and to ensure the necessary protection to avoid deterioration, including through the possible establishment of safeguard zones. This Article requires that the resulting water meets the minimum quality standards set by the Drinking Water Directive (DWD) (2).

Under the DWD, Member States must ensure that, by July 2027, a risk assessment and risk management is carried out in catchment areas for abstraction points, in relation to hazardous events that potentially cause harm to human health.

According to publicly available information, competent authorities assessed the potential impact of the project on water as part of the PAUR (3), which includes the EIA, and concluded that, based on strict conditions to avoid withdrawals and pollution impacts, the project would not entail a deterioration of the status of the affected water bodies (4).

It should be noted that INFR(2025)2207 and INFR(2026)2038 are not relevant for the matter at hand (5). The Commission has thus no evidence that the WFD has not been correctly applied by Italy in this case (6). In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors Member States compliance with EU law, focusing its enforcement action on systemic issues of non-compliance (7).
National courts are competent to verify compliance with EU law for individual cases.

Provvedimento Autorizzatorio Unico Regionale. The Lazio Region issued a positive opinion with conditions, finding the project compatible with the regional Water Protection Plan. Generally positive opinions or positive opinions with conditions were also issued by the Autorità di Bacino Distrettuale dell’Appennino Centrale and the Dipartimento III ‘Ambiente e Tutela del Territorio’ of the Rome Metropolitan City.

INFR(2025)2207 concerns the non-conform transposition of Article 11(3) WFD in Italy, and in particular the obligation to periodically review, and update, if needed, the controls over different types of water use, foreseen by Article 11(3)(e). INFR(2026)2038 concerns the non-conform transposition of various provisions of the DWD in Italy, which are not relevant for the case at hand.

With respect to the other two cases mentioned, the Commission refers the Honorable Members to its reply to Written Question E-002339/2026 regarding the Salone biodigester. Concerning the Casal Selce biodigester, it must be noted that the appeal mentioned is in front of the European Court of Human Rights and concerns compliance with the European Convention on Human Rights, so it is not relevant for the case at hand.
